paragraphs: I have shown that democracy favors the growth of manufactures and swells the ranks of the manufacturing classes without limit. Now we shall see by what indirect route manufacturers may in their turn lead men back to aristocracy. It is generally agreed that when a workman does the same small task every day, the whole product is made more easily, more quickly, and more cheaply. It is equally agreed that the cost of producing manufactured goods falls as the establishment that makes them grows larger, and as the capital or credit it employs grows greater. People had long glimpsed these truths only imperfectly, but in our time they have been proved. They have already been applied to many very important kinds of manufacture, and even the most humble will gradually come under their rule. I know of nothing in politics that deserves the lawmaker’s close attention more than these two new axioms of the science of manufactures.

A workman who spends all his time making one single thing eventually does that work with remarkable skill. At the same time, he loses the general ability to apply his mind to directing the work. Each day he grows more adept and less industrious, so that one may say of him that as the workman improves, the man is degraded. What can be expected of a man who has spent twenty years of his life making heads for pins? And what can that mighty human intelligence, which has so often stirred the world, be used for in him, except to find the best way of making pinheads? When a workman has spent a large part of his life like this, his thoughts are forever fixed on the object of his daily toil. His body has settled into fixed habits that it can never shake off. In a word, he no longer belongs to himself but to the calling he has chosen. It is in vain that laws and customs have taken the trouble to level every barrier around such a man and to open a thousand different roads to fortune before him on every side. A theory of manufactures more powerful than customs and laws ties him to a trade, and often to a place, that he cannot leave. It assigns him a certain position in society, beyond which he cannot go. In the midst of universal movement, it has left him standing still.

The more widely the principle of the division of labor is applied, the weaker, the narrower in mind, and the more dependent the workman becomes. The craft advances; the craftsman falls back. On the other hand, as it becomes more evident that manufactured goods are cheaper and better the larger the manufacture is and the more capital it employs, wealthy and educated men come forward to enter manufactures that used to be left to poor or ignorant craftsmen. The scale of the effort required and the importance of the results to be won attract them. So at the very time that the science of manufactures lowers the class of workmen, it raises the class of masters.

While the workman focuses his faculties more and more on a single detail, the master takes in a broader whole, and his mind expands as the workman’s shrinks. Before long the one will need nothing but physical strength without intelligence, while the other needs knowledge, and almost genius, to succeed. The master comes to resemble more and more the administrator of a vast empire, and the workman a brute. Master and workman thus have nothing in common here, and their differences grow every day. They are linked only like the two rings at either end of a long chain. Each fills the place made for him and cannot get out of it. The one is continually, closely, and necessarily dependent on the other, and seems as much born to obey as the other is born to command. What is this but aristocracy?

As the conditions of the men who make up the nation grow more and more equal, the demand for manufactured goods becomes more general and more extensive. The cheapness that puts these goods within reach of modest fortunes becomes a great element of success. So every day more men of great wealth and education devote their riches and knowledge to manufactures. By opening large establishments and enforcing a strict division of labor, they seek to meet the new demands arising on every side. Thus, as the mass of the nation turns toward democracy, the particular class engaged in manufactures becomes more aristocratic. Men grow more alike in the one and more different in the other, and inequality increases in the smaller class at the same rate at which it decreases in the community. Hence it would appear, if one searches to the bottom, that aristocracy should naturally spring from within democracy itself.

But this kind of aristocracy is in no way like those that came before it. One notices at once that, because it applies only to manufactures and to a few manufacturing callings, it is a monstrous exception in the general character of society. The small aristocratic societies that some manufacturers form amid the immense democracy of our age contain, like the great aristocratic societies of former ages, a few very wealthy men and a multitude of wretchedly poor ones. The poor have few ways to escape their condition and become rich. The rich, however, are constantly becoming poor, or they leave business once they have made their fortune. Thus the elements that make up the class of the poor are fixed, but those that make up the class of the rich are not. To tell the truth, though there are rich men, a class of rich men does not exist. These rich individuals have no feelings or aims in common, no shared traditions or hopes. There are therefore members, but no body.

Not only are the rich not closely united among themselves, but there is no real bond between them and the poor. Their relative position is not permanent; their interests constantly draw them together or pull them apart. The workman is generally dependent on the master, but not on any particular master. The two men meet in the factory but do not know each other anywhere else, and while they touch at one point, they stand very far apart on all others. The manufacturer asks nothing of the workman but his labor, and the workman expects nothing from him but his wages. The one takes on no obligation to protect, nor the other to defend, and neither habit nor duty joins them permanently. The aristocracy created by business rarely settles among the manufacturing population it directs. Its aim is not to govern that population but to use it. An aristocracy formed in this way can have no great hold on the people it employs. Even if it manages to keep them at one moment, they slip away the next. It does not know how to will, and it cannot act. The territorial aristocracy of former ages was bound by law, or believed itself bound by custom, to come to the aid of its servants and relieve their distress. But the manufacturing aristocracy of our age first impoverishes and debases the men who serve it, and then abandons them to be supported by public charity. This is a natural consequence of what has been said above. Between workmen and master there are frequent dealings, but no real partnership.

On the whole, I believe that the manufacturing aristocracy growing up before our eyes is one of the harshest that has ever existed in the world, but at the same time one of the most confined and least dangerous. Nevertheless, the friends of democracy should keep their eyes anxiously fixed in this direction. For if a permanent inequality of conditions and aristocracy ever enter the world again, it may be predicted that this is the channel by which they will come in.
